This is when one of the major nerves that provides sensation to your face—the trigeminal nerve—becomes irritated or compressed, causing it to send sudden, severe pain signals. It's often described exactly as you did: like an electric shock or a stabbing ice pick.

The fact that it's only on one side, triggered by things like wind or temperature, comes in brief episodes, and that your physical exam is normal all strongly point to this. The first line of treatment is medication. We typically use a specific type of nerve-stabilizing medication, like carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine. These are not regular painkillers like ibuprofen; they work by calming the overactive nerve. We would start at a low dose and adjust it carefully. Many people find excellent relief with this approach. How does that plan sound to you? I can answer any questions you have.
